column1: The Guild Hotel: heading structure recommendations for the new website
Based on the staging site (the-guild-hotel-c34e71.webflow.io), checked on 20 November 2026. One tab per page.
What this document is

This is an SEO recommendation for the heading tags (H1, H2, H3) on the new website. It is not a design change. Every change keeps the element's current class, so the page looks exactly the same as it does now.

We look at the page the way Google and AI search tools read it: through the code. The design team knows the build best, so please adjust anything that doesn't work technically. We're suggesting a structure, and we're happy to go through any line together.
Why the heading structure matters

Google and AI search tools (Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity) read the headings as the outline of the page. They use them to understand what the page is about and to split it into sections they can show in results or quote in an answer.

On the staging site most pages have 14 to 35 H2s, and the Arts page has 61. Many of them are slider cards, repeated offers, pop-up panels, the booking and newsletter blocks and the footer labels. That makes the outline unclear: the real sections of a page carry the same weight as "Stay in the loop" or a footer label.
Headings are also how screen reader users move around a page, so a clean structure helps accessibility as well.
To be fair about the size of this: a messy heading structure doesn't get a site penalised. It's a clarity signal, and it's quick to fix before launch.
The rules we follow
1. One H1 per page. It says what the page is about, ideally with the hotel name or the location.
2. One H2 for each main section of the page.
3. H3 for the items inside a section, such as dining venues, event spaces, rooms, articles and FAQ questions.

4. A paragraph (p) for anything styled like a heading that isn't a section title: slider card titles, repeated offers, pop-up panels, form field groups, booking and newsletter blocks and footer labels.
5. Each heading appears only once in the code. Hidden slides, tab panels, pop-ups and mobile copies count too, because Google reads them.
6. Type headings in normal case and let the CSS make them lowercase. Google and screen readers then read "Garden Terrace" instead of "garden terrace".
Shared parts: fix once, fixed everywhere

Several parts are the same on almost every page: the footer, the booking and newsletter block, the offers slider and the FAQ. They're listed on each tab so every page is complete, but each one only needs to be changed once in its component.
The 12 room pages share one template, and so do the 5 dining venue pages. Each has one tab.
How to read the page tabs
Keep: no change needed.
Change to p: the element is an H2 or H3 now and becomes a paragraph. Same class, same look.
Change div to H3 / Change p to H3 / Change p to H2: the element is plain text now and becomes a heading. Same class, same look.
Wrap logo in H3: the venue only shows a logo, so the logo goes inside an H3 and its alt text becomes the heading text.
Keep, update text: the tag is right, but we suggest adding the hotel name or location to the wording.
The Note for the designer column is only filled in where there's something specific to flag. Content notes at the bottom of each tab are not tag changes; they're points for the content team.
